nameStory: The green sea turtle gets its name from the green-colored fat beneath its shell, not from its shell color which is actually olive to black! This emerald fat comes from their unique diet of seagrass and algae. They're the only sea turtle that becomes a strict vegetarian as an adult.
description: Green sea turtles are massive marine reptiles with teardrop-shaped shells and powerful paddle-like flippers perfectly designed for ocean life. These gentle giants can grow quite large, with their smooth, flattened shells typically appearing olive-brown to black rather than green. They have relatively small heads compared to their body size and lack the hooked beak of some other sea turtles. In New England waters, you'd only spot these tropical visitors during warmer months as they follow ocean currents north.

idTips.label: Shell Shape
idTips.description: Large, smooth, teardrop-shaped shell (carapace) that feels surprisingly streamlined and lacks the bumpy ridges of other sea turtles

idTips.label: Flippers
idTips.description: Massive paddle-like front flippers that look almost wing-like underwater, much larger than the back flippers

idTips.label: Head Shape
idTips.description: Relatively small, rounded head with a blunt snout that lacks the sharp, hooked beak of hawksbill turtles

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Shell typically olive-brown to nearly black with lighter markings, not actually green despite the name

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Impressively large - one of the biggest sea turtles you might encounter, dwarfing any freshwater turtle

habitat: Green sea turtles are rare visitors to New England's coastal waters, typically spotted in warmer offshore areas during summer months. They prefer areas with eelgrass beds and kelp forests where they can graze, or may be seen near the surface in deeper waters following warm currents. Look for them around Stellwagen Bank, Cape Cod Bay, or other areas where warm Gulf Stream waters mix with local currents.

seasonality.spring: Very rare sightings as waters are still too cold for these tropical visitors.
seasonality.summer: Peak time for possible sightings in New England waters as they follow warm currents north to feed in seagrass beds.
seasonality.fall: May still be present in early fall but begin moving south as water temperatures drop.
seasonality.winter: Absent from New England waters - they've migrated to warmer southern waters or tropics.

funFact: Green sea turtles can hold their breath for up to 5 hours underwater, and some individuals may live to be 90 years old - meaning a turtle you spot today could have been swimming these oceans since the 1930s!
confusionNotes: In New England waters, most likely to be confused with loggerhead sea turtles, but green sea turtles have smaller heads, smoother shells, and lack the loggerhead's distinctively massive, blocky head. Remember: 'Green = streamlined, Loggerhead = big head.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'green' turtles, their shells are not green at all - this naming confusion has puzzled people for generations. The green refers to their internal fat color from their vegetarian diet, making them one of nature's most misleadingly named creatures.
compareHints: Green sea turtles are the only species in their genus Chelonia, making them unique among sea turtles. Compared to other sea turtles in New England waters like loggerheads, greens have more streamlined, smoother shells and smaller heads relative to body size. Unlike the omnivorous loggerheads, adult green sea turtles are strict vegetarians, giving them a more peaceful demeanor when observed.
